items.stem: Which is the best version of the underlined portion?
items.stimulus: In the early nineteenth century, Mary Anning searched the cliffs near Lyme Regis for fossils. Anning's work was physically demanding, but she continued examining the coast throughout the year. She recorded the location of each discovery, therefore, later researchers could compare her notes with those of other collectors. Her careful observations helped scientists understand that some fossils belonged to species unlike any living animals. Anning sold many specimens to visitors, and the income helped support her family. Local collectors valued Anning's discoveries, in turn, museums acquired several of her most important specimens. Scientists in London studied the fossils, in turn, their reports drew attention to the fossils' unusual features. Anning had little formal education, nevertheless, she learned to identify fossils by studying their structures. She also prepared <u>detailed drawings, and these illustrations</u> allowed distant scientists to examine specimens they could not visit. Her specimens changed scientific <u>discussions, consequently, later researchers</u> recognized that Earth's history was far older and more varied than many people had believed.
